responseDecisions.1.1: Preserve eight examples, five distortions and exact Claude substitution note. Separate confidence from categorical belief, multiple dimensions from a single gradient, legal city status from urban character, and moral evaluations from assumed moral facts. Retain response progression and make distortions conditional on relevant missing information.
responseDecisions.1.2: Preserve four examples and three limitations. Retain effective strangeness and qualifying-language passages; clarify suspension/disbelief, domain-specific expertise and administrative city status. Avoid unconditional agreement with the prompt.
responseDecisions.2.1: Preserve twelve-entry order and topics except the duplicated Intelligence item, explicitly replaced by Reliability. Explain multidimensional success/health/wealth, personality tendencies, addiction criteria and measurement uncertainty. Acknowledge deliberate revisiting of earlier concepts.
responseDecisions.2.2: Preserve twelve entries. Retain Old, Wet and Formal verbatim; correct clean-as-subjective, sweetness/sugar, busy/burnout, modernity-as-one-scale and health-as-total-verdict claims.
responseDecisions.3.1: Preserve eight problem areas and supply named primary evidence: EEOC settlement, Card/Giuliano screening, AMA BMI policy, Loving, Ofqual grades, Census SPM, youth hockey selection and Pew typology. Distinguish documented harms, institutional responses, measurement limitations and causal inferences; avoid claiming language alone caused outcomes.
responseDecisions.3.2: Preserve five areas. Add historical ACC definition change, EEOC employment dispute, gifted screening, Hall threshold and Loomis risk-score cautions. Replace erroneous uniform accomplice punishment claim; distinguish category decisions, underlying profiles and measurement uncertainty. Repeated cases intentionally develop the companion response.
responseDecisions.4.1: Preserve six criteria and five diagnostic questions, most verbatim. Improve precision/accuracy and novice explanations; add decision-changing-information test and distinguish eligibility result from capacity judgment.
responseDecisions.4.2: Preserve three uses, three reasons for detail and three balancing practices. Correct universal-symbol and nonexistent-yellow-light examples; distinguish categorical action from graded risk, use informative qualifiers, avoid medical totalization and explain multi-category thresholds.
responseDecisions.5.1: Keep five original subject areas. Supply clearly hypothetical headline patterns and concrete headline/body checks, with no invented quotes or frequency estimates. Distinguish distortion from proven intent; ordinary suffering language is not evidence of deception.
responseDecisions.5.2: Keep five numbered areas and two subitems per area. Restore sequential numbering. Improve celebrity uncertainty/relationship distinction, scientific evidence stages, localized weather risk and single-indicator economic claims. Do not attribute hypothetical examples to real outlets.
responseDecisions.6.1: Read every original question/key pair. Preserve ten items and ten answers at end. Replace ambiguous all-gradient multiple-choice options, unproved intent true/false claim, motive inference and subjectivity overgeneralization; align changed answers. Format options on separate lines.
responseDecisions.6.2: Read every original question/key pair. Preserve ten items and end key. Repair multiple valid least-binary options, mismatched media categories and implication that all concise signals are universal; align mental-health and headline answers. Format options on separate lines.
responseDecisions.7.1: Preserve fifteen questions, thirteen verbatim. Refine intentional simplification question and quantitative precision/uncertainty question; remove blanket motive claim from conclusion.
responseDecisions.7.2: Preserve fifteen questions, thirteen verbatim. Qualify media motive premise and replace false either/or about vocabulary evolution with a productive comparison.

research.scope: Full short EEOC settlement announcement, December 18 2020. Allegations and settlement distinguished from adjudicated findings; no independent litigation-file review.

Card and Giuliano 2016: abstract, opening study design and first results paragraphs. Verified unchanged eligibility standards and screening/referral distinction. No full statistical replication. NBER page returned403; original paper read through ERIC.
2023 policy announcement body on limitations, accompanying measures and insurance reimbursement; not a claim that BMI or weight labels alone cause eating disorders.
Original Loving opinion opening, factual background and statutory classifications. Official GovInfo PDF timed out; primary opinion text hosted by Cornell read instead.
Full short August17 2020 statement: distress, public confidence and decision to award higher of teacher/center estimate or calculated grade.
2011 SPM report opening two pages and indexed passage on taxes, transfers and expenses. No current poverty-rate claim or full report analysis.

Indexed original study abstract: 147991 male youth hockey players, selected/noncompetitive comparisons and qualified parental/coach explanation. Direct PubMed open returned a bare shell; no full-text claim.
2021 overview passages on nine groups, within-party heterogeneity and survey sample. No claim that this is the current typology or that the survey establishes label-induced polarization.
2017 announcement opening paragraphs, 32%/46% classification comparison and small medication increase. Explicitly historical classification example, not current treatment guidance.
Hall2014 syllabus and opinion opening; IQ71, rigid70 cutoff and measurement uncertainty. Earlier SupremeCourt slip PDF404; recovered official bound report.

Loomis2016 opinion opening, group/individual discussion and limitations at paragraphs44 and93–99. Affirmance and limited consideration distinguished from finding personal dangerousness. Not full opinion review.

originalPromptTexts: Many concepts that are intrinsically gradient are reflected in language with binary or granular terms that lack nuance. Provide a list of such terms including “belief”, “strange”, “expert”, and “city”. Elaborate on how the linguistic terms may distort the gradient nature of the underlying conceptual reality.
Provide an additional list of gradient concepts that are often reduced to binary or granular categories by linguistic terms.
Provide actual cases in which the use of an inadequate binary or granular term created real-life issues.
Discuss how we can determine whether a context is best served by a low-resolution binary term or by a more nuanced and conceptually precise high-resolution phrase.

The media is frequently guilty of intentionally employing low-resolution terms to loosely reflect gradient concepts to capture readership. Give 5 examples of this and highlight the clues this is being done.
Create a 10-item quiz on the discussion above with answers at the end.
Provide 15 discussion questions relevant to the content above.
